title: Finding ori
text:
The origin of replication (ori) is a specific DNA sequence at which DNA replication begins. It is the genomic region where the cellular machinery assembles and starts to synthesize new DNA strands. Due to its importance, there are experimental methods to elucidate the position of the ori-site, although this process takes time, effort, and expertise.
In recent years, 2nd- and 3rd-generation sequencing platforms have drastically reduced the time and cost to assemble draft genomes. Short sequencing reads allows for good genome depth while long reads reduce the uncertainty when building contigs from shorter sequences by increasing coverage. As a computational biologist, I would want to leverage this fact by finding ways to amortize the vast amounts of genomes published online.
Going back to the problem of ori finding, can we build heuristics for finding this region using only the genome sequence as input? We will dive into the ideas from Compeau’s and Pevzner’s book entitled Bioinformatics Algorithms: An Active Learing Approach and implement the algorithms in code.

title: Finding ori
text:
Genome Dataset
The goal is to develop heuristics that can be used to find the ori of bacterial genomes from sequence data alone. I will be using the Vibrio cholera genome as an example. First, let’s explore the properties of the genome by loading it into memory and computing a few properties such as length, base composition, and GC content.

# Load genome
genome_fp = "data/Vibrio_cholerae.txt"
with open(genome_fp, "r") as fh:
    genome = fh.read()

# Compute length
genome_length = len(genome)

# Compute base frequencies
base_freqs = {base: genome.count(base) for base in set(genome)}

# Compute GC content
gc_content = round((base_freqs['G'] + base_freqs['C']) / genome_length, 2)

Base counts: {'T': 294711, 'G': 256024, 'C': 263573, 'A': 293942}

title: Finding ori
text:
Expected K-mer Distribution
If we were to assume that the occurrence of DNA bases are uniformly distributed across a genome, the probability of observing a particular nucleotide at any position is given as:
\[ P(A) = P(T) = P(G) = P(G) = \frac{1}{4} \]
Under this model, the occurrence of nucleotide bases are assumed to be independent. Hence the probability of a sequence of k bases is simply the product of probabilities of each base:
\[ P(\text{k-mer}) = (\frac{1}{4})^k \]
We can then compute the expected frequncy of the k-mer using the formula:
\[ E = (L-k+1) \times (\frac{1}{4})^k \]


L = genome length






Example



How many ATGCG substrings are expected to occur in the V. cholerae genome?
\[ E = (1108250 - 5 + 1) \times (\frac{1}{4})^5 = 1082 \]
Under the null distribution, we expect any 5-mer to occur 1082 times.

title: Finding ori
text:
Frequent Words
In order to initate replication, DNA polymerase must somehow recognize and bind to the ori. This interaction is mediated by motifs, DNA sequences that have a higher affinity towards the binding domain of proteins. We can start to identify these motifs by finding the most frequent substrings of length k.

def most_frequent_kmer(genome: str, k: int):
    """Compute k-mer frequencies and return k-mer set with the highest counts"""
    L = len(genome)

    # Compute frequncies
    kmer_counts = {}
    for i in range(L-k+1):
        kmer = genome[i:i+k]
        if kmer in kmer_counts:
            kmer_counts[kmer] += 1
        else:
            kmer_counts[kmer] = 1

    # Compute maximum count
    max_count = max(kmer_counts.values())

    # Retain k-mers with counts equal to max_count
    max_kmers = []
    for kmer, count in kmer_counts.items():
        if count == max_count:
            max_kmers.append(kmer)

    return max_kmers









Figure 1: Number of most-frequent k-mers for k = 1…20





At \(k = 11\), we find 5 most-frequent k-mers. Is this result surprising? Let’s first check the sequences of the 11-mers.

title: Finding ori
text:
Asymmetry of Replication
DNA consists of two complementary strands that run in opposite (antiparallel) directions. One runs in the \(5' \to 3'\) (leading strand) direction while the other runs in the \(3' \to 5'\) (lagging strand) direction. Since DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides in the \(5' \to 3'\) direction, synthesis on the lagging strand is fragmented and discontinuous. This phenomenon leads to the formation of small gaps called Okazaki fragments.






Figure 2: Okazaki fragments in a replicating DNA strand



The transient single-stranded state of the lagging strand makes it unstable and more prone to mutation. It has been empirically confirmed that mutation rates are slightly higher for the lagging strand and this has been attributed to the spontaneous conversion of cytosine (C) to thymine (T), a phenomenon known as deamination.
As we move along the genome, we will observe a change in relative GC content. The frequency of cytosine will decrease in the forward half-strand due to deamination and increase in the reverse half-strand (Figure 3).






Figure 3: Schematic representation of the GC skew



We capture this information by keeping track of the running difference betwee the total counts of G and C. We then visualize the results in a skew diagram. Let’s plot the skew diagram for V. cholerae

import numpy as np

def skew(genome: str) -> np.array:
    """Compute the GC skew of a sequence"""
    L = len(genome)
    skew = np.zeros(genome_length+1)
    for pos, base in enumerate(genome, start=1):
        if base == "G":
            skew[pos] = skew[pos-1] + 1
        elif base == "C":
            skew[pos] = skew[pos-1] - 1
        else:
            skew[pos] = skew[pos-1]

    return skew









Figure 4: Genome skew of V. cholerae





As illustrated in Figure 3, the part of the graph where the skew transitions from decreasing to increasing is the ori (highlighted in green). The part where the skew goes from increasing to decreasing is the ter (highlighted in red), the region where replication stops or terminates.

title: Alignment-free Genome Comparisons
text:
Many sequence comparison workflows start with alignment, a computationally intensive task that scales quadratically with sequence length. Here, we explore an alignment-free method for comparing multiple genomes using k-mer counts. Put simply, a k-mer is a contiguous substring of a larger sequence with lenght k.
The workflow is as follows:

title: Alignment-free Genome Comparisons
text:
Data Retrieval
Three influenza strains and their corresponding genomes accessions are given below:



Strain
Accession

    --inputfile <(csvtk cut -Uf accession data/substypes.csv) \
    --include genome \

title: Alignment-free Genome Comparisons
text:
Genome Decomposition and K-mer Counting
In this step, we break down the genome sequence into its substrings of length k while keeping count of each unique substring. The bionumpy library provides the functionality for loading FASTA files and computng k-mer frequencies.

import bionumpy as bnp

# Load genome into memory
genome_fp = "data/ncbi_dataset/data/GCA_000820495.2/GCA_000820495.2_ViralMultiSegProj14656_genomic.fna"
record = bnp.open(genome_fp).read()

# Set k-mer size and alphabet
k = 3
alphabet = "ACGT"

# Compute complete k-mer set and initialize to zero
frequencies = {
    "".join(kmer): 0 
    for kmer in itertools.combinations_with_replacement(alphabet, k)
}

# Decompose into k-mers and compute frequencies
kmers = bnp.sequence.get_kmers(record.sequence, k)
counts = bnp.count_encoded(kmers, axis=None)
for kmer, count in zip(counts.alphabet, counts.counts):
    frequencies[kmer] = count

title: Alignment-free Genome Comparisons
text:
Visualization
We can inspect the distribution of k-mers by plotting their counts as a histogram.










Figure 1: Distribution of 3-mers of the Influenza genome




From Figure 1, we can observe that k-mers such as CCG, CGC, CGT, GCG, and TCG have low counts while AAA and GAA have high frequencies. Does this hint that the Influenza genome is AT rich?
Another way to visualize k-mer counts is thru a heatmap. To do this, we first reshape the counts array into a square matrix, then convert the frequencies to log-scale with pseudocounts.








Figure 2: 3-mer heatmap of the Influenza genome

title: Alignment-free Genome Comparisons
text:
Measuring Distance
The k-mer frequencies are represented as 4k-dimensional vectors. We can estimate the similarity of two genomes by computing a distance metric using their k-mer vectors. To remove the influence of genome size to the computed distance, we first normalize the elements then compute the L2 distance, also known as the Euclidean distance. I’ve packaged our previously implemented functions into a convenience class called KmerSet.

from scipy.spatial import distance

def extract_kmer_counts(ks: KmerSet):
    """Flatten k-mer counts into a row vector"""
    return np.array(list(ks.counts().values()))

def kmer_distance(ks1: KmerSet, ks2: KmerSet, metric: str = "euclidean"):
    """Compute the distance between two vectors containing k-mer counts"""
    counts1 = extract_kmer_counts(ks1)
    counts2 = extract_kmer_counts(ks2)

    # Normalize k-mer counts to remove genome size influence
    counts1 = counts1 / np.sum(counts1)
    counts2 = counts2 / np.sum(counts2)

    dist = None
    match metric:
        case "euclidean":
            dist = distance.euclidean(counts1, counts2)
        case "cosine":
            dist = distance.cosine(counts1, counts2)
        case "manhattan":
            dist = distance.cityblock(counts1, counts2)
        case _:
            dist = distance.euclidean(counts1, counts2)

    return dist

Computing the distances between pairwise comparisons of three Influenza genomes, we get the matrix in Figure 3.








Figure 3: Distance matrix of three Influenza genomes





The low distance values show the relatedness of the three genomes. This makes sense as all genomes are derived from the Influenza virus. However, we are still able to detect subtle differences between genomes by virtue of their k-mer compositions. Using the distances, we can conclude that Influenza A (GCA_000865725) has a genome that is more akin to Influenza C (GCA_000856665).

title: Methods for Comparing Strings
text:
The string matching problem, also called pattern matching, is a fundamental probelem in computer science and bioinformatics. It involves finding one or more occurrences of a pattern string P within a text or query string T. We denote the length of a given string s as \(|s|\).
Formally, the goal is to find all positions i in T such that:
\[ T[i..i+m-1] = P \]
The problem underlies many practical applications, such as:

Searching for DNA motifs or protein sequences in bioinformatics
Text searching in word processors or search engines
Plagiarism detection and data mining

Below, I will present a few algorithms to solve the pattern matching problem.

title: Methods for Comparing Strings
text:
The string matching problem, also called pattern matching, is a fundamental probelem in computer science and bioinformatics. It involves finding one or more occurrences of a pattern string P within a text or query string T. We denote the length of a given string s as \(|s|\).
Formally, the goal is to find all positions i in T such that:
\[ T[i..i+m-1] = P \]
The problem underlies many practical applications, such as:

Searching for DNA motifs or protein sequences in bioinformatics
Text searching in word processors or search engines
Plagiarism detection and data mining

Below, I will present a few algorithms to solve the pattern matching problem.

title: Methods for Comparing Strings
text:
Naive Exact Matching
The simplest, most straighforward solution is to simply align the start of pattern string P to the start of query string T and compare the characters of both strings index-wise. Once a mismatch occurs, we terminate the comparison since we already know that the two strings do not exactly match. After, we shift string P one character to the right and repeat the comparison. We do this until we reach the \(|T| - |P| + 1\) position where the last character of each string aligns. We illustrate this by finding the pattern brown within the text The quick brown fox:
The quick brown fox
brown brown
 brown brown
  brown brown
   brown brown
    brown brown
We find that there is a match between the pattern and the text at the 10th position. We can write a function that implements this comparison.

def naive_exact_match(p: str, t: str) -> list[int]:
    """Finds the starting positions where pattern (p) matches text (t)"""
    occurrences = []
    for i in range(len(t) - len(p) + 1):
        match = True
        for j in range(len(p)):
            if t[i+j] != p[j]:
                match = False
                break
        if match:
            occurrences.append(i)
    return occurrences

Passing in our query and text in the previous example, we get the following result:

p = "brown"
t = "The quick brown fox"
naive_exact_match(p, t)

[10]

title: Methods for Comparing Strings
text:
Boyer-Moore Algorithm
Similar to the exact matching algorithm, we slide pattern string P across text string T to perform our comparison. However, we compare characters from right to left at each alignment. In each alignment, we follow the bad character rule and the good suffix rule.

Bad Character Rule
Upon mismatch, skip alignments until (a) mismatch becomes a match, or (b) P moves past the mismatched character.






Example



Given text T = GCTTCTGCTACCTTTTGCGCGCGCGCGGAA, find the occurrences where pattern P = CCTTTTGC matches using the bad character rule




Step 1


T: GCTTCTGCTACCTTTTGCGCGCGCGCGGAA
P: CCTTTTGC


Shift to the right until \(C\) has a match. Skip 2 alignments.


Step 2


T: GCTTCTGCTACCTTTTGCGCGCGCGCGGAA
P: CCTTTTGC


Move P until it passes the current alignment. Skip 6 alignments.


Step 3


T: GCTTCTGCTACCTTTTGCGCGCGCGCGGAA
P: CCTTTTGC


All characters have been matched!




Good Suffix Rule
Let t = substring matched by inner loop; skip until (a) there are no mismatches between P and t or (b) P moves past t.


Step 1


T: CGTGCCTACTTACTTACTTACTTACGCGAA
P: CTTACTTAC


Shift P to the right until t has a match. Skip 3 alignments.


Step 2


T: CGTGCCTACTTACTTACTTACTTACGCGAA
P: CTTACTTAC


Move P until its prefix matches t. Skip 3 alignments.


Step 3


T: CGTGCCTACTTACTTACTTACTTACGCGAA
P: CTTACTTAC


All characters have been matched!



In Boyer-Moore matching, both the bad character and good suffix rules return the number of skips we can do in pattern matching. The decision in which rule to use is simply the one that yields a higher number of skips. We then shift our pattern P by our number of skips, then recompute a new skip count from the two rules. We repeat the process until we either find an exact match or reach the end of text T.
A caveat to this approach is that we need to build separate indexes from pattern P for both the bad character and good suffix rules. I won’t go into the detail of the pre-processing step, just think of it as a way to efficiently compute the number of shifts needed after evaluating an alignment. Explore the code is provided below:


Code
def build_bc_table(pattern: str) -> dict[str, int]:
    """Maps each character to its last index in the pattern"""
    bc = {}
    for i, c in enumerate(pattern):
        bc[c] = i
    return bc

def build_gs_table(pattern: str) -> list[int]:
    """Preprocess the pattern to create good suffix shift table."""
    m = len(pattern)
    gs = [0] * m
    border_pos = [0] * (m + 1)

    # Step 1: Precompute border positions
    i = m
    j = m + 1
    border_pos[i] = j

    while i > 0:
        while j <= m and pattern[i - 1] != pattern[j - 1 if j < m else 0]:
            if gs[j - 1] == 0:
                gs[j - 1] = j - i
            j = border_pos[j]
        i -= 1
        j -= 1
        border_pos[i] = j

    # Step 2: Precompute shifts for prefixes
    j = border_pos[0]
    for i in range(m):
        if gs[i] == 0:
            gs[i] = j
        if i == j:
            j = border_pos[j]

    return gs


We can now combine both rules to implement the Boyer-Moore algorithm.

def boyer_moore_search(text: str, pattern: str):
    """Boyer-Moore search using the Bad Character and Good Suffix heuristics"""
    n = len(text)
    m = len(pattern)
    if m == 0 or n == 0 or m > n:
        return []

    # Precompute indexes
    bc = build_bc_table(pattern)
    gs = build_gs_table(pattern)

    matches = []
    shift = 0

    while shift <= n - m:
        # Start from right-most position of current alignment
        j = m-1

        # Compare from right to left
        while j >= 0 and pattern[j] == text[shift+j]:
            j -= 1

        if j < 0:
            # Match found at index = shift
            matches.append(shift)
            # Shift so that next character after matched substring aligns
            shift += gs[0] if m > 1 else 1
            print(f"MATCH: shifting pattern to start at index {shift-1}")
        else:
            # Compute shifts
            bc_shift = j - bc.get(text[shift+j], -1)
            gs_shift = gs[j] if j < m - 1 else 1


            shift += max(bc_shift, gs_shift)
            if bc_shift > gs_shift:
                print(f"Using Bad Character rule: shifting by {shift} positions")
            else:
                print(f"Using Good Suffix rule: shifting by {shift} positions")

    return matches        


text = "AGTCGATGGCATTGATCGATTTTAGGCATTAGATCA"
pattern = "GGCAT"
boyer_moore_search(text, pattern)

Using Bad Character rule: shifting by 3 positions
Using Bad Character rule: shifting by 6 positions
Using Good Suffix rule: shifting by 7 positions
MATCH: shifting pattern to start at index 10
Using Good Suffix rule: shifting by 15 positions
Using Good Suffix rule: shifting by 19 positions
Using Good Suffix rule: shifting by 20 positions
Using Bad Character rule: shifting by 23 positions
Using Good Suffix rule: shifting by 24 positions
MATCH: shifting pattern to start at index 27
Using Good Suffix rule: shifting by 29 positions
Using Good Suffix rule: shifting by 33 positions


[7, 24]


In the example, the bad character heuristic always produced the most number of shifts for all alignment comparisons. The function detects that the pattern occurs at positions 7 and 24 of our text. Let us check if that is correct.

print("First match:", text[7:7+len(pattern)])
print("Second match:", text[24:24+len(pattern)])

First match: GGCAT
Second match: GGCAT
